en.title: Choosing a type
en.story: A desk counter holds the numeric value 2.5. The supplied output statement adds one and prints the result. Predict the value before running. In this lesson, + means numeric addition because both operands are numeric. Earlier you saw + join text in a welcome message. The same visible symbol can therefore depend on the kinds of values it receives. Start by deciding whether 2.5 is stored as a number or as quoted text; that distinction explains this small program's behavior.
en.idea: A type describes a kind of value. Numeric values support arithmetic, while strings represent text. Quotes around digits make a string in these examples; they do not ask the language to guess that you wanted a number. Java uses double for this fractional numeric value. JavaScript uses number, and TypeScript can state number explicitly. Python creates a float value from the unquoted decimal literal. These names differ, but the shared idea is numeric data rather than text. The language notes also explain whether your track reports a mismatch before running or during an operation.
en.make: Change the numeric starting value from 2.5 to 4.5. Keep the supplied addition and predict its new result. The exercise asks you to repair a value that was accidentally quoted. Locate the value's representation before changing the arithmetic. Removing quotes is appropriate for a numeric literal you write in source; it is not a method for converting text received as input. A later lesson introduces that separate conversion step. Check the first diagnostic or unexpected output rather than assuming all tracks reject the same mistake in the same way.
en.recap: The spelling of a value in source affects its kind. This example stores a numeric fraction, so adding one produces 3.5. A string containing digits is still text until a suitable conversion occurs. Java, Python, JavaScript and TypeScript differ in their type syntax and error behavior; use your track's note when a mismatch appears. Recall the numeric-versus-text distinction before looking at the cards. Next you will update a binding deliberately and trace which value is current at the moment it is printed.
